details:
This package is a fork of the Baileys WhatsApp Web library (npm) and belongs to the "PhantomSub" family described by OX Security in September 2026: the publisher injected code that, without the installer asking, uses the installer's own authenticated WhatsApp session to follow WhatsApp Channels (newsletters) the publisher chose.

`package/lib/Socket/messages-recv.js` line 45 defines a character-code decoder (`qvnr`). Lines 47-66 use it to build the channel identifier `120363428355171197@newsletter` and the method names `newsletterFollow` and `newsletterMute`, so none of them appears in the source as text.

Lines 1113-1138: 30 seconds after the connection opens, the library follows that channel and, 3 seconds later, mutes it.

`package/lib/Socket/newsletter.js` lines 86-115 also download a channel list from `u.pone.rs/oyptjqmf.json` after the connection opens, then follow and mute every channel in it. The publisher can change that list without publishing a new version. I did not fetch it.

The README does not mention it. The repository field names `FallEzz/cantarella-baileys`.

The hidden channel `120363428355171197@newsletter` is the same one `@nerxa/socketon`, `vp-baileys`, `xdc-baileys` and `wailib` follow.

Line numbers refer to version 1.1.16.

Static review of the published tarball found no code that sends WhatsApp credentials or session keys off-host, no install-time payload (the only install hook, where present, is Baileys' stock Node.js version check in `engine-requirements.js`), and no persistence; the payload runs when an application creates a WhatsApp socket with the library. The harm is the covert use of the victim's account to inflate the publisher's channel followers.

SHA-256 of the published npm tarball: 1.1.16: `da0fc74424abe6f5238605be3cc144358c5d9f05d356e16587be618de860d060`.
